verdicts.before: ASN.1 length field not validated against remaining input, allowing negative or oversized lengths :: readLength() only rejects a long-form length when `length >= limit`, but `limit` is the total buffer size, not the number of bytes remaining. In readSequence() the loop `while (length > 0)` subtracts `bytes.length` from the declared length; if readNext() returns fewer bytes than the declared length (e.g. because the inner element's length was itself inconsistent), the loop can spin or the outer length can go negative without error. More importantly, readInteger()/read(length) will allocate `new byte[length]` from an attacker-controlled length before any bounds check, so a malicious ASN.1 structure can trigger a large allocation (OutOfMemory) or a negative-length array. The `length < 0` check after the shift loop is dead for the 4-byte case because the shift can produce a negative int only when size==4 and the top bit is set, which is exactly the case that should be rejected but is instead silently accepted as a negative length that then flows into `new byte[length]`.

verdicts.before: result_processor instantiated before mode validation; queue_pool created with possibly uninitialized result_processor :: The `self.result_processor = self.result_processor_cls()` line was moved from the end of `__init__` to the top, before the mode branches. If `result_processor_cls()` raises or returns None for a subclass, the queue pool is created with a broken processor and no error surfaces until message processing. The new mode is only reachable via the exact string, and any typo silently degrades to serial processing with no warning. There is no test covering the invalid-mode path or the ordering of result_processor construction relative to queue_pool.

verdicts.before: Worker marks offset complete even when result_processor raises, silently dropping messages :: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the finally block calls offset_tracker.complete_offset regardless of whether result_processor succeeded. When result_processor raises (the except Exception branch logs and continues), the offset is still marked complete, so get_committable_offsets will advance past it and the message is committed without ever having been processed. The docstring on SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy claims 'Only commits offsets after successful processing', which this violates. Any transient error in the result processor (DB blip, downstream 5xx) causes permanent data loss for that group's message.

verdicts.before: Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash, so ordering is not stable across processes :: get_queue_for_group uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python string hashing is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same group_key maps to different queues in different consumer processes/restarts. The class docstring promises 'Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue', but during a rebalance or restart, in-flight items for a group can land on a different queue than the ones already queued, breaking the ordering guarantee the class exists to provide. It also makes queue distribution non-reproducible for debugging.
